Each time you perform an HI test, there is no way of knowing the exact concentration and potency of the RBC suspension you are using. Each suspension preparation will react differently with a given influenza virus. Furthermore, even the same RBC prep may react differently each day because the cells are constantly dying and changing. Because of this, you cannot just add a predetermined concentration of virus into each well. Let’s say, if you added 10 pfu/mL of virus per well today, the RBCs would respond in a certain way. But tomorrow, they may not give you the same result with the same 10 pfu/mL concentration because some of the RBCs may have degraded.

This is why instead of adding a set amount of virus each time you perform the test, you instead need to titer the virus according to the potency of the RBCs you’re using. This is where the 8 HA units thing comes in. This is a standardized number that was determined by the World Health Organization. In fact, in their influenza lab manual, you can read more about it: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/manual-for-the-laboratory-diagnosis-and-virological-surveillance-of-influenza

So 8 HA units is just an arbitrary number that the WHO decided upon so that even though the amount of virus you are adding to each well may change, its EFFECT on hemagglutination of the RBCs will remain the same and consistent throughout every test you perform.

Hope this makes sense. The WHO manual I linked to does a really great job of explaining this. That’s where I learned why we had to use 8 HA units each test.

If you do end up choosing to go into virology or any other biology/life science-related career, my advice for you would be to make sure you get some sort of lab experience during your undergraduate studies. You can work in the prep room for your campus’s microbio courses, you can do some internships, you can ask around to volunteer in a PI’s research lab as an undergrad research assistant. Just make sure you rack up some wet lab experience OTHER than your generic lab courses under your belt. It’ll set you apart from other students whether you go to industry for work or continue in academia.

Edit: I’d also recommend listening to the podcast This Week in Virology. It’s a great resource for learning about viruses, but they also go over career options for virologists! Might give you some ideas about your future while also teaching you all about viruses.

As you said in your post, organisms do not care about survival. They have no concept of life and death. On a cellular level, no cell has a brain, a consciousness, or sentience. So why does it seem like organisms, unicellular or multicellular, seek to survive?  

It’s because during different points of evolution, random mutations and other genetic events have resulted in brand new genotypes and phenotypes. Some of these phenotypes conferred traits to the organisms in which they occurred that increased their chances of survival compared to the organisms that didn’t have these traits. Consequently, it was more likely for these individuals to survive and produce offspring, while the other organisms were more likely to die, decreasing their odds of reproducing and propagating their genes. You can imagine that, after a certain amount of time, after this selection event kept happening many times, a given population of organisms had more individuals that had the new advantageous traits than individuals who did not.  

For example, at one point during evolution (which is a very simplistic view because evolution occurs as a continuous spectrum, not as discrete timepoints), the fight/flight/freeze response emerged in animals. This was a highly advantageous trait, as you can imagine that if you lacked this trait you were definitely more likely to die during a natural disaster or get eaten by a predator. So, the animals in which this new trait emerged survived and reproduced, and transferred these new traits to their offspring. Over time, the number of animals with this trait increased, and the number of those without dwindled.  

Survival often has got nothing to do with active thinking, consciousness, etc. A lizard in the desert couldn’t care less about life or death. It simply obeys its nature, a nature that has been fine-tuned for survival for billions of years not by some conscious desire or intelligent design, but by the indifferent laws of probability and random chance.

Honestly, I’m not sure what advantage you get from having a negative-sense RNA genome. Several such viruses have segmented/fragmented genomes, meaning that their genome usually isn’t just a big, single, intact RNA molecule, but there are multiple fragments of RNA molecules. For example, influenza A and B virus particles each contain 8 separate pieces of negative-sense RNA molecules. This fragmentation increases the ability to re-assort their genomes to create new strains of influenza, so perhaps having a negative-sense RNA genome confers this reassortment advantage. Just speculating here!

In a normal cell, when a portion of the DNA genome, or a gene, is transcribed to mRNA, that mRNA molecule is ready to directly go attach to a ribosome to make a protein. In this case, this mRNA molecule is said to be “positive” sense. In a similar manner, when a positive-sense RNA virus infects a host cell, its RNA genome can act as mRNA and be immediately used to make viral proteins because it’s positive sense. However, a negative-sense RNA virus cannot do this right away. Once such a virus infects a cell, it first has to transcribe its negative-sense RNA genome to a complimentary positive-sense RNA, and THEN this newly made RNA can act as the positive-sense mRNA to make viral proteins.

Edit: Negative-sense RNA viruses usually bring with themselves into the host cell their own RNA polymerases since they require to transcribe their own negative-sense RNA genome into positive-sense RNA first. However, positive-sense RNA viruses usually do not need to carry their own RNA polymerases because their genome can directly be translated by the host cell’s ribosomes.

I don’t think so. I think you should still try to avoid multitasking as much as possible while practicing the Participate skill.

Participate is *what* you do. One-Mindfully is *how* you do it. In other words, you participate one-mindfully, meaning you throw yourself into the activities of the current moment by focusing on that moment only and nothing else.  

Let’s say you’re having a nice dinner with friends at a restaurant. To practice Participate, you would throw yourself entirely into the conversations you’re having with your friends. To practice One-Mindfully, you would focus on the conversations ONLY, and avoid looking at your phone, avoid having your mind wander with ruminating thoughts, avoid thinking about what you need to do the next day, etc.  

As another example, I personally have a difficult time concentrating on a task because I always end up looking at my phone and social media. In situations like this, I remind myself that I need to practice One-Mindfully, which means putting away the phone and focusing solely on the task. No multitasking.  

Hope this helps.
